title: Reasoning and Proof
bigQuestion: How can a handful of accepted rules be enough to prove hundreds of facts about shapes?

story.title: Five Rules and Two Thousand Years
story.kicker: A teacher in ancient Alexandria wrote down five simple rules, and people are still arguing about the last one.
paragraphs: Around 300 BCE, in the city of Alexandria in Egypt, a mathematician named Euclid put together a book called the Elements. He did not invent most of the geometry in it. His real invention was the order. He began with a short list of definitions, five postulates and a few common notions, and then he proved everything else, one statement at a time, each resting only on the statements before it. Thirteen books later he had built up a whole world of lines, triangles, circles and solids from that tiny starting list.

The five postulates sound almost too simple to matter. You can draw a straight line between any two points. You can extend a segment into a longer line. You can draw a circle with any center and any radius. All right angles are equal to each other. The fifth one was different. It was long and wordy, and it described when two lines will eventually meet. Today we usually state it this way: through a point not on a line, there is exactly one line parallel to the given line. Readers felt that a rule that complicated ought to be provable from the other four.

For about two thousand years, mathematicians tried. They filled notebooks with attempted proofs, and every one of them quietly assumed the very thing it was trying to show. Then, in the 1800s, a few people asked a braver question: what if the fifth postulate is simply false? They replaced it with a different rule and followed the logic. Nothing broke. They had discovered new geometries, ones that describe curved surfaces, and those geometries later became the language physicists use to describe gravity and the shape of space.

The habit Euclid started, of asking what you are allowed to assume and then proving everything else, spread far beyond geometry. Abraham Lincoln, working as a lawyer in Springfield, Illinois, carried a copy of the Elements on the road and studied it by candlelight. He said he wanted to understand what it truly means to demonstrate something, to prove it so completely that no honest person could disagree. That is what this chapter is about: not just knowing that a fact is true, but showing exactly why.
story.think: Why would people spend centuries trying to prove a rule that everyone already believed was true? What did they gain when the attempt failed?

lessons.title: Points, Lines and Planes
lessons.mainIdea: Geometry starts with three undefined terms, and every other word is defined from them.
reading: Picture a map of Chicago. A bus stop is a dot on the map. Lake Shore Drive is a long straight stroke. The flat surface of Lake Michigan spreads out in every direction. In geometry these three pictures stand for the three undefined terms: *point*, *line* and *plane*. We describe them, but we never define them using other words, because every chain of definitions has to start somewhere. A point has no size, only a position. A line is perfectly straight, has no thickness, and continues forever in both directions. A plane is a flat surface with no edges.

Everything else gets a definition built from those three. A *segment* is the part of a line between two endpoints, like the stretch of Michigan Avenue between two cross streets. A ray starts at one endpoint and continues forever in one direction. Points that lie on the same line are *collinear*. Points that lie on the same plane are coplanar. When two different lines cross, they share exactly one point, called their intersection. Read each definition out loud the first time you meet it. A definition is a promise about what a word will mean every single time you use it.

Names matter. The line through points A and B is called line AB. Segment AB has endpoints A and B. In plain text, the length of that segment is also written AB, so you have to read carefully. Here is a common mistake: treating segment AB and the length AB as the same thing. One is a set of points you can draw. The other is a number, like 7 cm. Keep the object and its measurement separate in your head. Proofs later in this chapter become much easier when you know whether you are talking about a thing or a number.

words.d: an exact position with no size; one of geometry's undefined terms
a straight path with no thickness that goes on forever in both directions
a flat surface that extends forever in every direction, like an endless tabletop
the part of a line between two endpoints, including the endpoints
lying on the same line; three points are collinear if one line passes through all of them

look.title: How Many Lines?
look.text: Draw three points A, B and C that do not all lie on one line. Through each pair of points you can draw exactly one line: AB, BC and AC. That makes three lines. Now add a fourth point D that is not on any of those lines. The new lines are AD, BD and CD, so there are six lines in all. Each new point adds one line for every point already there.
look.prompt: How many lines would five points make if no three of them are collinear? Find the pattern before you count them all.

check.q: Which of these is an undefined term in geometry?
check.why: Point, line and plane are described but not defined. Segments, rays and angles are all defined using them.

check.q: Points A, B and C all lie on the same line. What word describes them?
check.why: Collinear means on the same line. Coplanar means on the same plane, which is true here too but is not the word for one line.

check.q: Segment PQ has endpoints P and Q, and PQ = 9 cm. Which statement is true?
choices: Segment PQ is a set of points, and PQ = 9 cm is its length
Segment PQ goes on forever in both directions
Segment PQ is a number and 9 cm is a set of points
check.why: The segment is the object made of points between P and Q. Its length, 9 cm, is a number that measures it.

lessons.title: Postulates and Theorems
lessons.mainIdea: A postulate is accepted without proof; a theorem must be proved from postulates, definitions and earlier theorems.
reading: Every game needs rules that players agree on before play begins. Geometry's starting rules are called postulates, and each one is a *postulate*. Some books call them axioms. A postulate is a statement accepted as true without proof. Euclid used five. One says that through any two points there is exactly one line. Another says a segment can be extended into a line. You cannot prove these from anything simpler. You accept them, and then you build.

A *theorem* is a statement that has been proved. The proof uses only definitions, postulates and theorems that were already proved. Here is a small one: if two different lines intersect, they intersect in exactly one point. Suppose two different lines shared two points, P and Q. Then both lines would pass through P and Q. But the postulate says exactly one line passes through two given points, so the two lines would have to be the same line. That contradicts the fact that they were different. So they can share at most one point. Notice how the proof leans on the postulate at the key moment.

Some postulates are about measuring. The *segment addition postulate* says that if point B is between A and C, then AB + BC = AC. Try it with algebra. Suppose AB = 3x, BC = 2x + 4 and AC = 29. Then 3x + 2x + 4 = 29, so 5x = 25 and x = 5. That gives AB = 15 and BC = 14. Check: 15 + 14 = 29. The angle addition postulate works the same way for two angles that share a side. A common mistake is to solve for x and stop. Read the question again. It may ask for AB, not for x.

words.d: a statement accepted as true without proof; a starting rule of geometry
a statement that has been proved using definitions, postulates and earlier theorems
if B is between A and C, then AB + BC = AC
another name for a postulate

look.title: Euclid's Common Notions
look.text: Things that are equal to the same thing are also equal to one another. If equals are added to equals, the wholes are equal. If equals are subtracted from equals, the remainders are equal. The whole is greater than the part.
look.cite: Euclid, Elements, Book I, the common notions, about 300 BCE (reworded from an early 1900s English translation)
look.prompt: Which common notion would you use to show that if AB = CD and CD = EF, then AB = EF? Which one lets you add BC to both sides of an equation?

check.q: Point M is between L and N. LM = 2x + 1, MN = 3x − 6 and LN = 40. What is LM?
check.why: 2x + 1 + 3x − 6 = 40 gives 5x − 5 = 40, so x = 9. Then LM = 2(9) + 1 = 19. The 9 is x, not LM, and 21 is MN.

check.q: What makes a statement a theorem rather than a postulate?
choices: It is about angles instead of segments
It has been proved from postulates, definitions and earlier theorems
check.why: Postulates are accepted without proof. Theorems are proved from them and from earlier results.

check.q: Point D is inside angle ABC. Angle ABD measures 35° and angle DBC measures 48°. What is the measure of angle ABC?
check.why: By the angle addition postulate, 35° + 48° = 83°. Subtracting gives 13°, which is the wrong operation.

lessons.title: Conjectures and Counterexamples
lessons.mainIdea: Inductive reasoning spots a pattern and makes a conjecture; deductive reasoning proves it; one counterexample disproves it.
reading: Stand at a bus stop every morning and watch. The bus comes at 7:05, then 7:20, then 7:35, then 7:50. You guess the next one arrives at 8:05. That is *inductive reasoning*: looking at several cases, noticing a pattern, and making a *conjecture*, which is an educated guess that might be true. Inductive reasoning is how most math ideas are born. But it is not proof. The bus schedule might change at 8:00.

*Deductive reasoning* starts from facts already accepted and reaches a conclusion that must follow. All right angles measure 90°. Angle X is a right angle. So angle X measures 90°. Here is a number example. Conjecture: the sum of two odd numbers is even. Inductive check: 3 + 5 = 8, 7 + 9 = 16, 11 + 1 = 12. Deductive proof: any odd number can be written 2m + 1, and another as 2n + 1. Their sum is 2m + 2n + 2 = 2(m + n + 1), which is 2 times a whole number, so it is even. The proof covers every odd pair at once, not just three of them.

A *counterexample* is one case where the pattern breaks. One is enough to sink a conjecture. Look at the formula n^2 + n + 41. For n = 1 it gives 43, for n = 2 it gives 47, for n = 3 it gives 53, for n = 4 it gives 61. All prime. It keeps producing primes for a long time, so a student might conjecture it always does. But when n = 40, the formula gives 1600 + 40 + 41 = 1681, and 41 × 41 = 1681. Not prime. Two common mistakes: believing that many examples prove a rule, and believing that one example proves it. Examples suggest. Proofs settle.

words.d: a statement you believe is true based on a pattern, but have not proved
reasoning from specific examples to a general pattern
reasoning from accepted facts to a conclusion that must follow
one example that fits the hypothesis but breaks the conclusion, proving a conjecture false

look.title: Values of n^2 + n + 41
look.prompt: The first five values are all prime. Is 1681 prime? What does that single row do to the conjecture that the formula always gives a prime?

check.q: A student sees 1, 4, 9, 16, 25 and predicts that 36 comes next. What kind of reasoning is this?
check.why: The student looked at examples and found a pattern. That is inductive reasoning. A proof would be deductive.

check.q: Which number is a counterexample to the claim that every number divisible by 4 is also divisible by 8?
check.why: 12 ÷ 4 = 3, so 12 is divisible by 4, but 12 ÷ 8 is not a whole number. The other choices are divisible by both.

check.q: Conjecture: if a number is prime, then it is odd. Which statement is correct?
choices: The number 2 is a counterexample, so the conjecture is false
The conjecture is true because most primes are odd
check.why: 2 is prime and even. One counterexample is enough to make the conjecture false, no matter how many primes are odd.

lessons.title: Conditional Statements
lessons.mainIdea: A conditional has a hypothesis and a conclusion, and it is false only when the hypothesis is true and the conclusion is false.
reading: If it rains on Saturday, then the game is canceled. That sentence is a *conditional statement*. The part after if is the *hypothesis*: it rains on Saturday. The part after then is the *conclusion*: the game is canceled. Mathematicians write a conditional as p → q, read as if p then q. Many geometry facts hide their if-then shape. Vertical angles are congruent really means: if two angles are vertical angles, then they are congruent. Rewriting a fact in if-then form shows you exactly what you are assuming and exactly what you are claiming.

When is a conditional false? Only in one situation: the hypothesis happens and the conclusion does not. It rains, and the game is played anyway. That breaks the promise. If it does not rain, the promise was never tested, so the statement is still counted as true. Try a number example. If x = 3, then x^2 = 9. That is true, since 3 × 3 = 9. Now flip it: if x^2 = 9, then x = 3. That is false, because x could be −3, and (−3) × (−3) = 9 too. The first statement makes a promise it keeps. The second makes a promise it breaks.

Two common mistakes. First, assuming the hypothesis always comes first in the sentence. You pass the class if you earn 60 percent puts the hypothesis at the end: earning 60 percent is the if part. Second, treating a conditional as if it works both ways. A conditional only promises one direction. The *negation* of a statement, written not p, says the opposite. The negation of x is greater than 5 is x is not greater than 5, which includes x = 5. Watch that edge case.

words.d: an if-then statement, written p → q
the if part of a conditional statement; what is assumed
the then part of a conditional statement; what is claimed to follow
the opposite of a statement; the negation of 'it is raining' is 'it is not raining'

look.title: Find the If and the Then
look.text: Three sentences from everyday life: (1) A student who scores 90 or above earns an A. (2) All squares have four congruent sides. (3) You may check out a book when you show a library card. Each one is a conditional in disguise.
look.prompt: Rewrite each sentence in if-then form. Which part is the hypothesis and which is the conclusion? Is each statement true when the hypothesis is false?

check.q: In the statement 'If a polygon has three sides, then it is a triangle,' what is the hypothesis?
check.why: The hypothesis is the if part: a polygon has three sides. The conclusion is that it is a triangle.

check.q: When is a conditional statement false?
choices: when the hypothesis is true and the conclusion is false
check.why: A conditional promises the conclusion whenever the hypothesis holds. It fails only when the hypothesis happens and the conclusion does not.

check.q: Which conditional statement is false?
choices: If a shape is a square, then it has four sides
If an angle measures 90°, then it is a right angle
check.why: x = −5 also gives x^2 = 25, so the hypothesis can be true while the conclusion is false. The other three always hold.

lessons.title: Converse, Inverse, Contrapositive
lessons.mainIdea: The contrapositive always matches the original statement's truth; the converse and inverse can be different.
reading: Start with a true statement: if a number ends in 0, then it is divisible by 5. Now build three relatives. The *converse* swaps the two parts: if a number is divisible by 5, then it ends in 0. False, because 15 is divisible by 5 and ends in 5. The *inverse* negates both parts: if a number does not end in 0, then it is not divisible by 5. Also false, and 15 is again the counterexample. The *contrapositive* swaps and negates: if a number is not divisible by 5, then it does not end in 0. True. Every number ending in 0 is divisible by 5, so a number that is not divisible by 5 cannot end in 0.

That pattern is not a coincidence. A conditional and its contrapositive are *logically equivalent*: they are always both true or both false. Think about the rain promise. If it rains, the game is canceled. Suppose the game is not canceled. Then it must not have rained, or the promise would have been broken. So, if the game is not canceled, then it did not rain. Same promise, stated backward. The converse and inverse are also equivalent to each other, but neither is tied to the original.

In geometry this matters because converses often need their own proofs, and some converses are false. If two angles are vertical angles, then they are congruent: true. The converse, if two angles are congruent then they are vertical angles, is false, since two separate 30° angles are congruent without being vertical. When a proof seems stuck, try proving the contrapositive instead. Showing that not q leads to not p proves the original just as well. A common mistake is to assume a true statement's converse is automatically true. Check it separately, every time.

words.d: the statement formed by swapping the hypothesis and conclusion: if q then p
the statement formed by negating both parts: if not p then not q
the statement formed by swapping and negating both parts: if not q then not p
two statements that are always both true or both false, like a conditional and its contrapositive

look.title: Four Versions of One Statement
look.text: Original: if a quadrilateral is a square, then it has four right angles. Write the converse, the inverse and the contrapositive. A rectangle that is 3 cm by 5 cm has four right angles but is not a square. Use that rectangle to test each version.
look.prompt: Which of the four statements are true? Which pairs always agree with each other, and why does the 3 by 5 rectangle break the ones it breaks?

check.q: What is the converse of 'If two angles are complementary, then their measures add to 90°'?
choices: If two angles are not complementary, then their measures do not add to 90°
If two angles' measures do not add to 90°, then they are not complementary
If two angles' measures add to 90°, then they are complementary
Two angles are complementary if and only if their measures add to 90°
check.why: The converse swaps the hypothesis and conclusion without negating anything. Here it happens to be true, because that is the definition.

check.q: Which statement always has the same truth value as the original conditional?
check.why: A conditional and its contrapositive are logically equivalent. The converse and inverse match each other, not the original.

check.q: Original: 'If a number is a whole number, then it is an integer.' This is true. What is the inverse, and is it true?
choices: If a number is not a whole number, then it is not an integer; false, since −3 is an integer but not a whole number
If a number is an integer, then it is a whole number; true
If a number is not an integer, then it is not a whole number; false
If a number is not a whole number, then it is not an integer; true
check.why: The inverse negates both parts. It fails because −3 is not a whole number but is an integer.

lessons.title: Biconditionals and Definitions
lessons.mainIdea: A biconditional is true when a conditional and its converse are both true, and every good definition is a biconditional.
reading: Two lines are *perpendicular lines* if and only if they meet at a right angle. The phrase *if and only if* means the statement runs both ways. If the lines are perpendicular, they meet at a right angle. And if they meet at a right angle, they are perpendicular. A statement of this shape is a *biconditional*, written p ↔ q. It is true only when the conditional and its converse are both true. If either direction fails, the biconditional is false.

Every good *definition* is a biconditional, even when it is not written that way. A right angle is an angle that measures 90°. Read forward: if an angle is a right angle, it measures 90°. Read backward: if an angle measures 90°, it is a right angle. Both hold, so the definition works. Now test a bad one: a square is a quadrilateral with four right angles. Forward is fine, since every square has four right angles. Backward fails: a 3 by 5 rectangle has four right angles but is not a square. So that sentence is not a definition of a square. It describes a rectangle.

Here is an algebra biconditional: x + 5 = 12 if and only if x = 7. Forward: subtract 5 from both sides, and x = 7. Backward: 7 + 5 = 12. Both directions work, so the biconditional is true. Compare it with x^2 = 49 if and only if x = 7. Backward is fine, since 7^2 = 49. Forward fails, because x = −7 also gives 49. That biconditional is false. The common mistake is writing if and only if when only one direction has been checked. Always test both.

words.d: a statement that combines a conditional and its converse, written p ↔ q
the phrase that shows a statement is true in both directions
a statement of exactly what a word means; it must work as a biconditional
two lines that meet to form a right angle

look.title: Testing a Definition
look.text: A student proposes this definition: a midpoint is a point that lies on a segment. Forward: if M is a midpoint of segment AB, then M lies on AB. That is true. Backward: if M lies on segment AB, then M is a midpoint of AB. Picture AB as 10 cm long, with M placed 2 cm from A.
look.prompt: Does the backward direction hold? Fix the proposed definition so that both directions are true, and check your new version with the 10 cm segment.

check.q: Which conditional can be rewritten as a true biconditional?
choices: If a triangle has three congruent sides, then it is equilateral
If two angles are vertical angles, then they are congruent
If an animal is a dog, then it has four legs
check.why: Equilateral means three congruent sides, so the converse is also true. The others have false converses: x = −4, congruent angles need not be vertical, cats have four legs.

check.q: The biconditional 'x − 3 = 10 if and only if x = 13' is:
choices: true only in the forward direction
check.why: Forward: add 3 to both sides, x = 13. Backward: 13 − 3 = 10. Both directions work.

check.q: Why is 'A square is a quadrilateral with four right angles' not a good definition?
choices: Squares do not have right angles
A 2 by 5 rectangle has four right angles but is not a square, so the converse fails
check.why: A definition must work both ways. The rectangle is a counterexample to the backward direction.

lessons.title: Two-Column Proofs With Segments
lessons.mainIdea: A two-column proof lists statements on the left and a reason for each on the right, from the given to what you want to prove.
reading: You already write proofs when you solve equations; you just do not label the reasons. Solve 3x + 7 = 22. Statement 1: 3x + 7 = 22. Reason: *given*. Statement 2: 3x = 15. Reason: subtraction property of equality, since subtracting 7 from both sides keeps the equation true. Statement 3: x = 5. Reason: division property of equality. That is a *two-column proof*. Every line on the left has a reason on the right, and each reason is a definition, a postulate, a property or a theorem. Other properties you will use: the *reflexive property* (a = a), the symmetric property (if a = b then b = a), the *transitive property* (if a = b and b = c then a = c) and the *substitution property* (if a = b, you may replace a with b anywhere).

Now a segment proof. Points A, B, C and D lie on a line in that order. Given: AB = CD. Prove: AC = BD. Line 1: AB = CD, given. Line 2: BC = BC, reflexive property. Line 3: AB + BC = CD + BC, addition property of equality, since we added the same length to both sides. Line 4: AB + BC = AC and CD + BC = BD, segment addition postulate. Line 5: AC = BD, substitution. Check it with numbers: put A at 0, B at 2, C at 5 and D at 7. Then AB = 2 and CD = 2, while AC = 5 and BD = 5. The proof says it works for any positions, not just these.

Three habits keep proofs honest. Every statement needs a reason, even the obvious ones. The word given may only be used for facts the problem handed you. And you may never use the statement you are trying to prove as a reason along the way, because that is circular. A common mistake is skipping the reflexive line, BC = BC. It looks silly, but without it there is nothing to justify adding BC to both sides.

words.d: a proof written as numbered statements on the left with a reason for each on the right
a fact the problem states as true; the starting point of a proof
any quantity equals itself: AB = AB
if a = b and b = c, then a = c
if two quantities are equal, one can replace the other in any statement

look.title: The Proof With Numbers
look.text: Points A, B, C and D lie in that order on a line. AB = 4, BC = 6 and CD = 4. Compute AC by adding AB + BC, and compute BD by adding BC + CD. Then move the points: make AB = 9, BC = 1 and CD = 9, and compute both again.
look.prompt: Do AC and BD come out equal both times? Which line of the two-column proof explains why they must be equal whenever AB = CD?

check.q: Which property justifies this step: if AB = CD and CD = EF, then AB = EF?
check.why: The transitive property links two equalities that share a middle term. Substitution would also work, but transitive names this exact pattern.

check.q: In a two-column proof that if 2x − 5 = 11 then x = 8, what is the reason for the step 2x = 16?
check.why: Adding 5 to both sides of 2x − 5 = 11 gives 2x = 16. That is the addition property of equality.

check.q: Points P, Q, R and S lie in that order on a line, and PQ = RS. Which statement is proved by adding QR to both sides?
check.why: PQ + QR = PR and QR + RS = QS by the segment addition postulate, so PR = QS.

lessons.title: Angle Proofs
lessons.mainIdea: Angle proofs rest on two facts: a linear pair adds to 180°, and vertical angles are congruent.
reading: Two streets cross, and four angles appear at the corner. Two angles that share a side and whose other sides form a straight line are a *linear pair*. The linear pair postulate says their measures add to 180°, so they are *supplementary*. Angles that add to 90° are *complementary*. The two angles across from each other at the crossing are *vertical angles*. Number the four angles 1, 2, 3, 4 going around. Angles 1 and 3 are vertical, and so are 2 and 4.

Here is the proof that vertical angles are congruent, and it uses only the linear pair postulate. Angles 1 and 2 form a linear pair, so m∠1 + m∠2 = 180°. Angles 3 and 2 also form a linear pair, so m∠3 + m∠2 = 180°. Both sums equal 180°, so m∠1 + m∠2 = m∠3 + m∠2 by substitution. Subtract m∠2 from both sides: m∠1 = m∠3. That is the subtraction property of equality. Try it with numbers. If vertical angles measure (3x + 10)° and (5x − 30)°, set them equal: 3x + 10 = 5x − 30, so 40 = 2x and x = 20. Each angle is 70°. Its linear pair partner is 180° − 70° = 110°.

The same subtraction trick proves two more theorems. If two angles are supplementary to the same angle, they are congruent, because each one equals 180° minus that angle. If two angles are complementary to the same angle, they are congruent for the same reason with 90°. Two common mistakes: setting vertical angles equal to 180° instead of equal to each other, and assuming two angles are congruent because they look alike in a drawing. In a proof, a picture is a hint, not a reason.

words.d: the two opposite angles formed when two lines cross; they are always congruent
two adjacent angles whose outer sides form a straight line; their measures add to 180°
two angles whose measures add to 180°
two angles whose measures add to 90°

look.title: One Angle Gives All Four
look.text: Two lines cross, forming angles 1, 2, 3 and 4 in order around the point. Angle 1 measures 52°. Angle 2 is its linear pair partner, so angle 2 measures 180° − 52° = 128°. Angle 3 is vertical to angle 1, and angle 4 is vertical to angle 2.
look.prompt: Find angles 3 and 4, then add all four measures. Why should the total be 360° no matter what angle 1 measures?

check.q: Two vertical angles measure (4x + 6)° and (6x − 20)°. What is x?
check.why: Vertical angles are equal: 4x + 6 = 6x − 20, so 26 = 2x and x = 13. Setting the sum to 180° gives 19.4, a common error; 58 is the angle measure.

check.q: Angles 1 and 2 form a linear pair. Angle 1 measures 115°. What does angle 2 measure?
check.why: A linear pair adds to 180°, so 180° − 115° = 65°. The 25° comes from wrongly using 90°.

check.q: Angle A is supplementary to angle C, and angle B is also supplementary to angle C. What can you conclude?
choices: angle A is congruent to angle B
angle A and angle B are supplementary
angle A is congruent to angle C
check.why: Both A and B equal 180° minus angle C, so they are congruent. That is the congruent supplements theorem.

lessons.title: Paragraph and Flow Proofs
lessons.mainIdea: Paragraph, flow and two-column proofs carry the same statements and reasons in different layouts.
reading: A *midpoint* is the point that divides a segment into two congruent segments. Claim: if M is the midpoint of AB, then AM = 1/2 AB. Here it is as a *paragraph proof*, which is a proof written in sentences. Since M is the midpoint of AB, AM = MB by the definition of midpoint. By the segment addition postulate, AM + MB = AB. Substituting AM for MB gives AM + AM = AB, so 2 AM = AB. Dividing both sides by 2 gives AM = 1/2 AB. Every sentence names its reason, exactly as a two-column proof would.

A *flow proof* shows the same logic as boxes connected by arrows, so you can see which facts feed into which. One box holds M is the midpoint of AB (given). An arrow leads to AM = MB (definition of midpoint). A second starting box holds AM + MB = AB (segment addition postulate). Both arrows meet at 2 AM = AB (substitution), which leads to AM = 1/2 AB (division property). Flow proofs are useful when two separate chains of reasoning join at one conclusion, because the arrows show the joining.

Check the result with numbers. If AB = 18, then AM should be 9, and 9 + 9 = 18. Now use it in algebra: M is the midpoint of AB, with AM = 3x + 2 and MB = 5x − 8. Since AM = MB, 3x + 2 = 5x − 8, so 10 = 2x and x = 5. Then AM = 17, MB = 17 and AB = 34. The most common mistake in paragraph proofs is dropping the reasons because the sentences flow smoothly. A paragraph proof is still a proof. Every claim has to say why.

words.d: a proof written in sentences, where each statement still names its reason
a proof drawn as boxes joined by arrows that show which statements lead to which
the point on a segment that divides it into two congruent segments

look.title: Three Layouts, One Proof
look.text: Given: M is the midpoint of segment AB, AM = 2x + 7 and MB = 4x − 5. Prove: AB = 38. Start by setting 2x + 7 = 4x − 5, because a midpoint makes AM = MB. Solve for x, find AM, then use the segment addition postulate to reach AB.
look.prompt: Write the argument first as a paragraph proof and then as a flow proof. Do the two versions need any different reasons?

check.q: M is the midpoint of AB. AM = 2x + 3 and MB = 4x − 9. What is AB?
check.why: 2x + 3 = 4x − 9 gives x = 6, so AM = 15. AB = AM + MB = 15 + 15 = 30. The 6 is x and 15 is only half.

check.q: What does a flow proof use instead of numbered rows?
choices: boxes joined by arrows that show which statements lead to which
check.why: A flow proof arranges statements in boxes and uses arrows to show the logical path from givens to the conclusion.

check.q: Which statement about paragraph proofs is true?
choices: They do not need reasons because they are written in sentences
They can only prove facts about segments
Each statement still needs a reason, written into the sentences
They are less valid than two-column proofs
check.why: The layout changes, but the logic does not. Every claim in a paragraph proof must state the definition, postulate or theorem behind it.

lessons.title: Parallel Lines and Transversals
lessons.mainIdea: When a transversal crosses parallel lines, corresponding angles are congruent, and that one fact proves the other angle pairs.
reading: Chicago's streets mostly run in a grid, with east-west streets parallel to each other. A few diagonal streets, like Milwaukee Avenue, slice across the grid. A line that crosses two or more other lines is a *transversal*. Where a transversal crosses two lines, eight angles appear, four at each crossing. Number them 1 through 4 at the top crossing and 5 through 8 at the bottom, in the same order. Angles in the same position at each crossing, like 1 and 5, are *corresponding angles*. Angles between the two lines on opposite sides of the transversal, like 3 and 6, are *alternate interior angles*. Angles between the lines on the same side, like 3 and 5, are *consecutive interior angles*.

The corresponding angles postulate says: if the two lines are *parallel lines*, then corresponding angles are congruent. From that one rule we can prove the rest. Claim: alternate interior angles 3 and 6 are congruent. Angle 2 corresponds to angle 6, so ∠2 ≅ ∠6. Angle 2 and angle 3 are vertical angles, so ∠2 ≅ ∠3. By the transitive property, ∠3 ≅ ∠6. Consecutive interior angles are supplementary by a similar chain: ∠3 ≅ ∠6 as just shown, and angles 6 and 5 form a linear pair, so m∠3 + m∠5 = m∠6 + m∠5 = 180°.

Now some numbers. Alternate interior angles measure (2x + 15)° and (3x − 20)°. They are congruent, so 2x + 15 = 3x − 20 and x = 35. Each angle is 85°. A consecutive interior angle next to one of them measures 180° − 85° = 95°. The converses also hold and are how we prove lines parallel: if corresponding angles are congruent, or alternate interior angles are congruent, or consecutive interior angles are supplementary, then the lines are parallel. Two mistakes to avoid: assuming lines are parallel because they look parallel in a sketch, and setting consecutive interior angles equal when they should add to 180°.

words.d: a line that crosses two or more other lines
angles in the same position at each crossing of a transversal; congruent when the lines are parallel
angles between the two lines on opposite sides of the transversal; congruent when the lines are parallel
angles between the two lines on the same side of the transversal; supplementary when the lines are parallel
two lines in the same plane that never meet

look.title: A Diagonal Across the Grid
look.text: A diagonal avenue crosses two parallel east-west streets. At the northern crossing, the angle on the northeast side measures 118°. Label the eight angles and use vertical angles, linear pairs and corresponding angles to fill in the rest.
look.prompt: What are the measures of all eight angles? How many different measures appear, and why only that many?

check.q: Two parallel lines are cut by a transversal. A pair of consecutive interior angles measure (2x)° and (x + 30)°. What is x?
check.why: Consecutive interior angles are supplementary: 2x + x + 30 = 180, so 3x = 150 and x = 50. Setting them equal gives 30, a common error.

check.q: Two parallel lines are cut by a transversal. One of a pair of alternate interior angles measures 74°. What is the other?
check.why: Alternate interior angles between parallel lines are congruent, so the other is also 74°. The 106° would be a consecutive interior angle.

check.q: Which fact lets you conclude that two lines cut by a transversal are parallel?
choices: a pair of vertical angles are congruent
a pair of consecutive interior angles are congruent
a pair of alternate interior angles are supplementary
a pair of corresponding angles are congruent
check.why: The converse of the corresponding angles postulate proves lines parallel. Vertical angles are always congruent, so they say nothing about parallelism.

lessons.title: Compass and Straightedge
lessons.mainIdea: A construction uses only a compass and an unmarked straightedge, and every step is backed by a postulate or theorem.
reading: Euclid's first three postulates describe two tools. A *straightedge* draws a line through two points; it has no marks, so it cannot measure. A *compass* draws a circle or arc with a chosen center and radius. A *construction* is a drawing made with only those two tools. Start with copying a segment: draw a ray, set the compass to the length of the original segment, and swing an arc from the ray's endpoint. Where the arc crosses the ray is the copy's other endpoint. No ruler needed.

Next, the *perpendicular bisector* of segment AB. Open the compass wider than half of AB. Draw an arc from A, then an arc of the same radius from B. The arcs cross at two points, one above the segment and one below. Draw the line through those two points. Why does it work? Each crossing point is the same distance from A as from B, because both arcs used the same radius. A point equidistant from A and B lies on the perpendicular bisector, so the line through two such points is the bisector. It cuts AB at its midpoint and meets it at 90°.

To draw an *angle bisector*, swing an arc from the vertex V so it crosses both sides at points P and Q. Then draw equal arcs from P and Q that meet at a point R inside the angle. Ray VR splits the angle in half. Triangles VPR and VQR have three pairs of equal sides, which, as the next chapter proves, makes them congruent and their angles at V equal. To draw a line through a point parallel to a given line, copy an angle so that corresponding angles are congruent. Not everything is possible: mathematicians proved in the 1800s that no compass-and-straightedge construction can cut a general angle into three equal parts. The most common construction mistake is changing the compass width between two arcs that must match.

words.d: a geometric drawing made using only a compass and an unmarked straightedge
a tool for drawing straight lines; it has no marks for measuring
a tool for drawing circles and arcs with a chosen center and radius
the line that passes through a segment's midpoint at a right angle
a ray that divides an angle into two congruent angles

look.title: Why the Arcs Must Reach
look.text: Segment AB is 6 cm long. Set the compass to 2 cm and try the perpendicular bisector construction: the arc from A reaches only 2 cm out, and the arc from B reaches only 2 cm out, so they never touch. Set the compass to exactly 3 cm and the arcs touch only at the midpoint, giving one point instead of two. Now set it to 4 cm.
look.prompt: Why does the construction need the compass opened to more than half of AB? What goes wrong with one crossing point instead of two?

check.q: When bisecting segment AB with arcs, why must the arcs from A and B have the same radius?
choices: so the crossing points are equidistant from A and B, which puts them on the perpendicular bisector
so the arcs are the same color
check.why: Equal radii make each crossing point the same distance from both endpoints. Such points lie exactly on the perpendicular bisector.

check.q: Which tools are allowed in a classical construction?
choices: a ruler with inch marks and a protractor
an unmarked straightedge and a compass
check.why: Euclid's postulates allow only drawing lines through points and circles with a given center and radius: straightedge and compass.

check.q: To construct a line through point P parallel to line m, you should:
choices: measure 90° with a protractor at P
draw a circle centered at P
copy an angle so that corresponding angles are congruent
fold the paper along line m
check.why: Congruent corresponding angles guarantee parallel lines by the converse of the corresponding angles postulate. Copying an angle uses only compass and straightedge.

review.q: Point B is between A and C. AB = 4x − 3, BC = 2x + 5 and AC = 38. What is BC?
What is the contrapositive of 'If a figure is a square, then it is a rectangle'?
choices: If a figure is a rectangle, then it is a square
If a figure is not a square, then it is not a rectangle
If a figure is not a rectangle, then it is not a square
A figure is a square if and only if it is a rectangle
review.why: The contrapositive swaps and negates both parts. It is true, just like the original.

review.q: Which value of x is a counterexample to 'If x^2 > x, then x > 1'?
review.why: (−2)^2 = 4, and 4 > −2, so the hypothesis holds, but −2 > 1 is false. For 1/2, the hypothesis fails, so it is not a counterexample.

review.q: Two angles form a linear pair and measure (3x + 12)° and (2x − 7)°. What is x?
review.why: A linear pair adds to 180°: 5x + 5 = 180, so x = 35. Setting them equal gives 19, which is the wrong relationship.

review.q: Two parallel lines are cut by a transversal. Corresponding angles measure (3x)° and (x + 80)°. What is the measure of each angle?
review.why: Corresponding angles are congruent: 3x = x + 80, so x = 40 and each angle measures 3(40) = 120°. The 40 is only x.

review.q: In a proof, what is the reason for the statement AB + BC = AC when B is between A and C?
review.why: The segment addition postulate says the two pieces add up to the whole segment.

review.q: Which statement is a true biconditional?
choices: A number is even if and only if it is divisible by 2
x^2 = 16 if and only if x = 4
Two angles are congruent if and only if they are vertical angles
A quadrilateral is a square if and only if it has four right angles
review.why: Even means divisible by 2, and both directions hold. The others each have a false direction: x = −4, congruent non-vertical angles, and rectangles.

review.q: A proof that vertical angles are congruent, built from the linear pair postulate, is an example of:
review.why: The proof starts from an accepted postulate and reaches a conclusion that must follow. That is deductive reasoning.
